name: Safety razor

lead: A safety razor holds a single replaceable double-edge blade behind a guard in a reusable handle. Wet-shaving fans use it for a close shave, smoother skin and fewer razor bumps than with cartridges, on the face and body.

The blade protrudes a fixed amount past the guard, cutting at the skin surface, and a single blade avoids the tug-and-cut action of multi-blade cartridges. A reported 2024 near-infrared imaging study found less post-shave redness than with a three-blade cartridge. Head-to-head trials on ingrown hairs are lacking.

paras: Users soften hair with warm water, apply a lubricating cream or gel, and shave with light pressure in short passes, usually with the grain. Blades are swapped regularly and are cheaper than cartridges. Technique and preparation matter more than the razor.

It can cut or irritate with poor technique, and nicks are common while learning. Dermatology reviews on shaving bumps advise softening hair first, avoiding very close passes and using lubricating gel, whatever the razor.

social.title: I shaved my face with a safety razor for the first time

web.title: I shaved my face with a safety razor for the first time - Lemmy

angle.text: Wet-shaving hobbyists and forum users prefer safety razors for a close shave and report fewer ingrowns and razor bumps than with cartridges. A single blade and a guard shave at the surface for smoother skin. A 2024 imaging study reportedly found less redness than a three-blade cartridge.

lead: A safety razor is a razor in which a thin replaceable blade, usually double-edged, is clamped in a reusable handle behind a guard that limits how far the edge contacts the skin.[1][2] It sits between the open straight razor and the modern multi-blade cartridge, and it is favored by wet-shaving hobbyists, for example on forums such as Badger & Blade, and by some users on looksmax.org who treat a clean, close, low-irritation shave as part of facial presentation.[3][4][5]

The appearance payoff proponents describe is a smooth, even shave with fewer nicks, less redness and fewer ingrown hairs, which makes the jawline and skin look cleaner, along with low running costs because blades are cheap.[5][6] A 2024 near-infrared imaging study reportedly found less post-shave redness with a safety razor than with a three-blade cartridge, but head-to-head trials on ingrown hairs are lacking, and dermatology reviews place most of the weight on preparation and technique rather than razor type.[7][8]

The safety razor has a documented commercial history that runs from an 18th-century French guard razor through King Camp Gillette's disposable double-edge blade, patented in 1904 and mass-marketed from 1903, to a revival among hobbyists in the 21st century.[2][9][10] Procter & Gamble estimated in 2010 that almost a billion men used double-edge razors worldwide, according to Wikipedia.[2]
infobox: King C. Gillette; company founded 1901, sales from 1903[9][10]
Straight bar, open comb, adjustable, slant[2]
Blade replacement; handle lasts for years

paras: The blade is clamped between a guard plate and a cap, with the edges partly enclosed so hair enters the narrow gap while the guard bar controls skin contact.[1] This differs from a straight razor, which has an exposed blade that needs honing, and from cartridge razors that integrate several blades in a disposable head.[1][2]

Wikipedia groups safety razors into single-edge, double-edge and cartridge or disposable forms. Single-edge razors have been made by makers such as American Safety Razor (Ever-Ready) and Gem; injector razors let users insert blades without handling them. Double-edge razors come from makers such as Edwin Jagger, Feather, Merkur, Mühle and Weishi, with head designs including a straight safety bar, open comb, adjustable head and slant bar, plus a twist-to-open butterfly design and three-piece razors with interchangeable handles.[2]
Razor steel is low in chromium and can be very sharp but corrodes easily; drying blades and washing off skin salts is said to prolong their life, and some users strop blades on denim.[2]

Wikipedia says the French cutler Jean-Jacques Perret likely invented the guard razor around 1762, adding a protective guard modeled on the joiner's plane to a straight razor.[2] In 1847 William S. Henson patented a hoe-shaped razor with a comb-tooth guard, and in 1880 Frederic and Otto Kampfe of Brooklyn patented the design sold as the Star Safety Razor, the first attested use of the term safety razor.[2] The stated aim of these guards was to reduce the skill needed for injury-free shaving and the reliance on barbers.[2]

King Camp Gillette, born in 1855 in Fond du Lac, Wisconsin, conceived a razor with a thin disposable blade stamped from carbon steel sheet. Machinist Steven Porter built the first working blade from Gillette's drawings, and William Emery Nickerson redesigned the frame and designed production machinery and blade-hardening methods.[9] Gillette founded the American Safety Razor Company on 28 September 1901, renamed Gillette Safety Razor Company in 1902 according to one Wikipedia article and 1904 according to another.[9][10] The company sold 51 razors and 168 blades in 1903, its first year of production, and 90,884 razors and 123,648 blades the next year.[9] A patent for a razor with disposable double-edge blades was granted in 1904.[1][2]

During World War I, Gillette supplied US troops with about 3.5 million razors and 32 million blades; returning soldiers kept the razors and created steady demand for blades.[2][10] Wikipedia notes that barbers' share of shaving revenue fell from about 50 percent around 1898 to about 10 percent by 1939.[11] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that patent expiry in 1921 spurred competition, a detail not confirmed elsewhere.[1]

The cartridge era followed. Wilkinson Sword began selling stainless steel blades in 1962, forcing American makers to respond, then launched a bonded cartridge in 1970; Gillette's twin-blade Trac II followed, Bic launched the fully disposable razor in 1974, and Gillette's triple-blade Mach3 arrived in 1998, followed by four- and five-blade models.[2][10] Double-edge razors remained in production, and Gillette launched a King C. Gillette beard-care line in May 2020 that included a double-sided safety razor.[10]

Wikipedia's article on wet shaving describes the usual sequence: soften the hair with warm to hot water or a hot towel, apply lather or another lubricant, shave in several light passes that remove a little hair at a time, shave in the direction of growth, avoid pressing hard, and finish with an optional aftershave, with an alum block or styptic pencil available to close small cuts.[11] The same article says multiple passes are meant to reduce cuts, soreness and ingrown hairs, and that razor burn is attributed to blunt blades, dry shaving, pressure or shaving against the grain.[11]

Hobbyist communities add tools and variables: a shaving brush and bowl for lather, shaving soaps and creams, a choice of blade brand (users often say the best blade depends on the razor and the individual's beard), and different razor aggressiveness, from mild fixed heads to adjustable models. In a 2020s Lemmy thread a first-time user reported a less close shave than usual but less irritation and two nicks, and replies advised light pressure, careful blade angle, thorough lathering and trying different blades.[12]

According to Grokipedia's summary, a multispectral near-infrared spectroscopy study of 59 men found less shaving-induced erythema with a safety razor than with a three-blade cartridge (40.3% versus 57.6% of skin areas).[1][7] That is the only description of the study's results available to cite here, and it concerns redness, not ingrown hairs.

Claims of fewer ingrown hairs are common in shaving communities and Grokipedia repeats them, but no independent controlled trial comparing razor types for ingrowns was found. A 2019 review of pseudofolliculitis barbae reports that multi-blade razors are commonly linked to the condition, because the first blade is thought to pull the hair so that the cut tip retracts below the skin, and it also notes a recent report blaming improper technique more than blade count.[8]

sections.h: Razor bumps, razor burn and technique
paras: Pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps) is an inflammatory reaction in which a shaved hair curls back into or alongside the follicle. Wikipedia says it most affects people with curly or thick facial hair and that growing a beard is the most effective prevention; for those who keep shaving it suggests a sharp single-blade razor replaced each shave, leaving a little stubble, shaving every other day with the grain and softening the beard first.[13] The 2019 treatment review describes two mechanisms, hair tips growing sideways through the skin after a very close shave and cut tips retracting into the follicle when the skin is stretched or shaved against the grain, and recommends warm water, a clean sharp razor, shaving with the grain and not stretching the skin.[8] It does not single out safety razors, and it describes electric clippers with a guard and laser hair removal as other options.[8][13]

That review lists dry shaving, blunt blades, stretching the skin, shaving against the grain and infrequent shaving as risk factors.[8] Safety razors can still cut or nick the skin, and the guard does not remove that risk.

A 1977 comparison for preoperative hair removal found that both razor and electric clipper damaged the skin surface, while a depilatory caused a mild reaction.[14] Case literature records razor use as a predisposing factor in axillary hidradenitis suppurativa.[15] Wikipedia notes that cuts can bleed for around fifteen minutes and that acne makes cuts more likely.[11] Razor steel corrodes easily if left damp, according to Wikipedia.[2]

Wet-shaving forums host threads on beginners' setups, comparisons with electric shavers and shaving against the grain.[3][4][16] On looksmax.org, safety razors appear within long wet-shaving guides titled around irritant-free skin and avoiding razor bumps, where authors describe warm-water preparation, soap or cream, light pressure and aftershave routines.[5][6] Their stated goal is a close shave without irritation or razor bumps.[5][6]

Related options include straight-razor shaving, cartridge razors, electric foil and rotary shavers, beard trimmers set to a short length, depilatories and laser hair removal for people prone to razor bumps.[8][2][13] Wet shaving is also paired with alum blocks, styptic pencils and aftershave.[11]

One 2024 study of razor design and shaving-induced erythema compared razor types (see Effectiveness).[7] A 1977 comparative study examined razor, clipper and depilatory for surgical hair removal.[14] A 2019 review summarises treatment of razor bumps without comparing safety razors with cartridges.[8] No trial was found comparing safety razors with cartridges for ingrown hairs.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, safety razors appear within long wet-shaving guides that promise less irritation and fewer razor bumps than disposable or cartridge razors.[5][6]

claims.claim: Wet shaving gives a closer, less irritating shave than dry shaving
Double-edge or single-blade razors suit thick beards better than cartridge razors
